lesson.title: Resistance in series
lesson.orientation: Follow one closed path through two resistors and predict what changes when one resistor gets larger.

visualBrief.learningPurpose: Show that two resistors in one closed path add to a total resistance while carrying one shared current.
facts: The wire forms one closed path.
Two resistors are connected one after another.
The equivalent resistance is the sum of the resistor values.
The same current passes through each resistor in an ideal series circuit.

objects.name: First resistor
objects.description: The first resistor in the single path.

objects.name: Second resistor
objects.description: The second resistor in the single path.

forbiddenElements: Unequal current labels in the same path
visualBrief.altTextDraft: A battery connects to two labelled resistors in one closed loop. An arrow shows one current path through R1 and R2.
verificationChecks: There are exactly two resistors and no branch.
The total resistance is the sum of the two resistor values.
The calculated current agrees with 9 V divided by 300 Ω.

lesson.nextAction: Open the next lesson to see what changes when the path divides into branches.

steps.headline: Resistors one after another add their resistances.

lead.text: Charge has to push through each resistor in turn, so the opposition builds up. Resistors joined end to end on one path are in series.
A 100 Ω resistor then a 150 Ω resistor oppose the flow like one 250 Ω resistor.
A 9 V battery drives a loop with a 100 Ω resistor, then a 200 Ω resistor. The loop has only one path.
A meter beside each resistor counts the charge passing it each second.

reveal.text: The same. Series components share one current. What they don't share equally is the voltage, which comes next.

steps.headline: Each resistor takes a share of the battery's voltage, and the shares add to the battery's voltage.

lead.text: The current is the same, but a bigger resistance needs a bigger push to pass it. The voltage across a resistor is its current times its own resistance: V = I × R, which is Ohm's law turned round.
In a 6 V loop where one resistor takes 2 V, the other takes the remaining 4 V.

steps.headline: An 8 V battery drives a 150 Ω and a 250 Ω resistor in series. Find the current.

workedSteps.text: Charge passes each resistor in turn, so add the resistances.
Apply Ohm's law to the total.

steps.headline: A 9 V battery drives a 100 Ω and a 200 Ω resistor in series. Find the current.

workedSteps.text: Apply Ohm's law to the total.

lead.text: This one is only about the total. Same method, no current needed.

reveal.text: Add the two values. Series resistances always add, and a longer chain always has a larger total.

lead.text: The same circuit idea, asked about voltage this time. Find the current first, then use V = I × R.

visualStates.caption: Two resistors, one after another, on a single loop.

blocks.text: A 10 V battery drives 0.1 A through one 100 Ω resistor.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the current when resistors share one path, and say how the battery's voltage divides between them.

recap.keyIdea: In series the resistances add and one current passes every component. The battery's voltage divides, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

blocks.text: You added 220 Ω and 330 Ω to get 550 Ω, and found that 9 V across 300 Ω drives 0.03 A through both resistors.

recap.nextHook: Let the path divide into branches. Which of these rules survive?

questions.prompt: A third resistor is added to an existing series circuit, along the same single path. What happens to the total resistance?
hints: Recall how series resistances combine.
A third resistor adds another term to that combination.
Decide whether adding a positive term raises or lowers the total.

acceptedIdeas: it rises by the value of the new resistor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises by the value of the new resistor.

choices.label: It rises by the value of the new resistor
It falls below the smallest resistance in the path
It stays the same because the path is unchanged
It becomes the average of the three resistances

questions.onCorrect: Each added resistor adds its own value, so a third one always raises the total.

misconceptions.feedback: A new resistor adds opposition. It can't take the total below what was already there.
The path is longer for the charge now: a third resistor adds to the total.
Series resistances add. An average would be smaller than the sum.

questions.prompt: Calculate I = 9 V ÷ 300 Ω, in amperes.
hints: Divide the voltage by the total resistance.
The total resistance is already worked out: 300 Ω.
Work out 9 ÷ 300.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rtotal = 100 Ω + 200 Ω = 300 Ω; I = V / Rtotal = 9 V / 300 Ω = 0.03 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.03 A. The total resistance sets the current for the whole loop.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses only one of the resistors. Both oppose the flow, so use their total.

questions.prompt: A 220 Ω resistor and a 330 Ω resistor are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance, in ohms.
hints: Resistors one after another add their resistances.
Write R total = R1 + R2 with the two given values.
Add 220 and 330.
questions.onCorrect: 550 Ω. In series the resistances simply add.

misconceptions.feedback: Resistances in series add; they don't subtract.
Resistances in series add; they aren't multiplied.

questions.prompt: Two unequal resistors are connected in series across a battery. Explain what this does to the current in each resistor and to the voltage across each one.
hints: Start from how many routes the charge has through a series pair.
Decide whether the current can differ between two components on one route.
Then say how the supply voltage is shared between unequal resistances.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two resistors sit in a single path, so the same current passes through both. The voltage divides between them, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

questions.onCorrect: One path gives one current. The voltage divides, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

questions.prompt: A 10 V battery drives 0.1 A through one 100 Ω resistor. A second 100 Ω resistor joins the same wire, one after the other. What is the current now, in amperes?
hints: Two resistors in a row oppose the flow more than one.
Ohm's law still gives the current as V ÷ R. What is R now?
Treat the pair as one 200 Ω resistor and divide.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two resistors oppose the flow like 200 Ω, so I = 10 V ÷ 200 Ω = 0.05 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.05 A. The second resistor doubles the opposition, so the same battery drives half the current.

misconceptions.feedback: Two resistors oppose the flow more than one, so the current should fall, not rise.
That is the current with one resistor. The second one adds opposition.

questions.prompt: A meter beside the 100 Ω resistor reads 0.03 A. What does a meter beside the 200 Ω resistor read, in amperes?
hints: How many routes does charge have around this loop?
Could charge leave the path between the two resistors?
Recall what you found about current in a single loop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One path, so the same current passes both resistors: 0.03 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.03 A. A single path carries a single current, whatever the resistors are.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger resistance holds the flow back for the whole loop. It does not use current up on its own side.
The larger resistor does not make more charge pass. One path means one current.

hints: Think about the route the charge takes.
Does the charge meet one resistor or both?

acceptedIdeas: Charge has to get through each resistor in turn
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Charge has to get through each resistor in turn.

choices.label: Charge has to get through each resistor in turn
Each resistor has a battery of its own
The resistors share the current equally

questions.onCorrect: Charge meets the resistors one after another, so their opposition builds up along the single path.

misconceptions.feedback: There is one battery in the loop. Ask what the charge meets as it goes round.
Sharing current is true, but it doesn't explain adding. Think about what the charge passes through on its way round.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives a 100 Ω resistor and a 200 Ω resistor in series. What is the voltage across the 200 Ω resistor, in volts?
hints: Find the total resistance first, then the current.
The voltage across a resistor is the current times its own resistance.
The current is 12 ÷ 300. Multiply it by 200.
questions.onCorrect: 8 V. The larger resistor takes the larger share, and the two shares add back to 12 V.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of the smaller resistor. Check which resistor the question asks about.
The battery's voltage isn't split equally. A bigger resistance takes a bigger share.
That is the current. The question asks for the voltage across the 200 Ω resistor.

questions.prompt: A 6 V battery is connected to a 100 Ω resistor and a 500 Ω resistor in series. Calculate the current, in amperes.
hints: Add the two resistances first.
Divide the battery voltage by that total.
Work out 6 ÷ 600.
questions.onCorrect: 0.01 A. Add the resistances, then let Ohm's law work on the total.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses only the 100 Ω resistor. Both resistors are in the path.
That uses only the 500 Ω resistor. Both resistors are in the path.

questions.prompt: What is the total resistance of a 10 Ω and a 20 Ω resistor in series, in ohms?
hints: Resistors in series add.
Write R1 + R2 with the two values.
Add 10 and 20.
questions.onCorrect: 30 Ω. In series the resistances add.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one resistor's value. Both are in the path, so both count.
That multiplies the two values. Series resistances add.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery drives two resistors in series. One has 5 V across it. How many volts are across the other?
hints: The two drops add back to the battery's voltage.
Take the known drop away from the supply.
Work out 9 − 5.
questions.onCorrect: 4 V. The voltage drops add back to the battery's 9 V.

misconceptions.feedback: The drops are not equal here. They add to the battery's voltage.
The whole battery voltage is shared between the two. Neither resistor gets all of it.
